guidance: A nominal gauge-to-thickness lookup for sheet metal, not a measurement: gauge tables differ by metal, mills roll within a tolerance and coated or polished sheet varies, so confirm a critical thickness with a micrometer or the mill certificate.
method: A sheet-metal gauge number is a weight-based designation, not a length, and each metal has its own table. Uncoated carbon steel uses the Manufacturers' Standard Gauge, where the decimal thickness is the nominal weight per square foot divided by 41.82 lb/ft2 per inch, which is why 10 gauge is 0.1345 in and 16 gauge is 0.0598 in. Galvanized sheet repeats the steel gauge with the zinc coating included, 0.0037 in more than the uncoated sheet (the allowance the distributors' tables apply under ASTM A653 practice), and no galvanized gauge 7 is published. Stainless sheet has its own table, a little thicker than carbon steel at the same number: 16 gauge is 0.0625 in and 26 gauge is 0.0187 in. Aluminum sheet follows the Brown & Sharpe, or American Wire Gauge, series, so 16 gauge is only 0.0508 in. The page covers gauge 7 to 30 in all four systems; heavier sheet is normally ordered by decimal thickness. Decimal inches are converted to millimetres at exactly 25.4 mm per inch and shown to three decimals, with the inches kept to four. A whole number in the input is read as a gauge (16, 16 ga, gauge 16, #16); a number followed by mm or in, or a bare number with a decimal point, is read as a thickness. For a thickness, the nearest gauge in each table is the row with the smallest absolute difference in millimetres, with a tie going to the lower gauge number, and the difference is reported in millimetres and as a percentage of the entered thickness. A value within half a thousandth of a millimetre of a published row is called exact. Every figure is nominal: gauge tables are not tolerances, suppliers sometimes quote their own conversion, and coating weight, rolling tolerance and polishing move the real thickness, so a critical part needs a micrometer or the mill certificate. The page does no structural, load or weight calculation and runs entirely in the browser.
